source.title: OrthoEraser: Coupled-Neuron Orthogonal Projection for Concept Erasure
source.authors: Chuan-Cheng Shi; Wenhua Wu; Fei Shen; Xiaogang Zhu; Kun Hu; Zhi-Yong Wang

record.file_problem: Full paper and supplementary material are present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses SAE feature disentanglement and feature entanglement as premises for a concept-erasure method, but its main results evaluate erasure and image quality rather than whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs.
record.gate_note: The paper describes zero-ablation activation shifts to identify coupled features; this related result is recorded with versions ["none"] because it does not measure the unrelated-input responses or other behavior specified by V1–V7. Erasure counts, image-quality scores, and activation-amplification results are omitted because they report the performance of the erasure method, not polysemanticity.
record.test_reason: The study assumes superposition and entanglement and builds an SAE-based concept-erasure method for text-to-image models. It reports erasure counts, FID and CLIP scores. It does not measure whether individual neurons respond to unrelated inputs, what causes such responses, or how common they are. The coupled-neuron activation-shift analysis is a property of SAE re-encoding, not neuron polysemanticity.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that projecting SAE-derived sensitive directions onto the null space of coupled benign features gives a better safety–fidelity trade-off than prior erasure baselines. The base-model measures are I2P detections reduced from 646 to 5 and FID 1.15.
record.recipe_differences: A text-to-image concept-erasure method using SAE features, zero-ablation coupling detection, and orthogonal projection; it does not use the original sources' neuron-polysemanticity measurement.
record.method_sensitivity: Erasure outcomes vary with intervention layer and suppression factor λ; the paper also reports results across several model architectures, but these are erasure and utility outcomes rather than polysemanticity measures.

fits_no_version.finding: In SD1.4's text encoder, zero-ablating sensitive SAE features and re-encoding produces large, long-tailed activation shifts in some benign SAE features. Other features stay near zero. This is shown qualitatively in Fig. 7.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features in T2I text encoders are non-orthogonal, so removing some features' decoder contributions perturbs re-encoded activations of a subset of other features.

record.problems: The activation-shift result is reported qualitatively without numerical values in the text. It does not establish that coupled features respond to unrelated inputs, and the paper notes that its method depends on SAE dictionary capacity and reconstruction fidelity.
record.rows_left_out: Erasure detections, image-quality metrics, layer and λ ablations, cross-model erasure results, and activation-amplification results are in Tables 1–5 and Figures 5–11. They were omitted because they evaluate concept-erasure performance or image quality, not the claim versions' measures of polysemanticity.

untested.parts: No MLP neurons of language models examined. Only SAE features on the text-encoder layer of T2I models.
Superposition is assumed as motivation (non-orthogonal superposition) but not tested as a cause of polysemanticity.
No comparison of polysemantic-neuron share across architectures or activation functions. The cross-model results are erasure performance only.

record.verdict_notes: Peer-review status of 'European Conference on Computer Vision' is not supported by the text. The arXiv v1 shows no venue. Polysemantic activations are mentioned only as a premise for using SAEs.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test whether neurons in image classifiers respond to several unrelated inputs.
Does not study transformer language-model MLP neurons or token/context responses.
Invokes superposition and entanglement but does not test whether polysemanticity is caused by capacity pressure or feature packing.
Does not test initialization, regularization, or training noise as causes of polysemanticity without capacity pressure.
Does not compare polysemantic-neuron prevalence across activation functions, architectures, or regularization settings.
Does not establish that canonical mixed responses share one feature or job, or that unrelated mixtures are rare.
Does not compare polysemanticity judgments across activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods.

rows.subject: SD1.4
rows.operation_detail: Zero-ablate sensitive features, re-encode activations, and measure shifts in coupled benign neurons.

conditions.value: sensitive prompt set; size not stated

rows.measure: Activation shift (δ) of coupled benign neurons after sensitive-feature zero-ablation
rows.value: The paper reports that coupled neurons have large-magnitude, long-tailed activation shifts.
rows.note: The paper presents this as evidence of feature entanglement and collateral perturbation. It does not show that the coupled features correspond to unrelated input meanings or assess polysemanticity as defined in V1–V7.
rows.check: The shift (δ) is measured on SAE features after subtracting decoder directions and re-encoding. It reflects non-orthogonality of the SAE basis, not neurons responding to unrelated inputs. It is reported only qualitatively (Fig. 7), with no numbers. The subject is the SD1.4 text-encoder layer 10 SAE features. The state relative to any version cannot be determined.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
